title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that “AI literacy” has become a prominent but inconsistently defined concept, especially after the rise of generative AI. The authors ask how researchers conceptualize and approach AI literacy in K-12 and higher education, and what trends have emerged since generative AI became publicly available. Rather than evaluating one intervention, the paper synthesizes a broad and heterogeneous body of literature to clarify the field’s changing definitions, goals, and pedagogical approaches.

The study uses an integrative review methodology to analyze 124 empirical and theoretical studies published between 2020 and July 2024. The authors searched ERIC and Scopus, supplemented this with purposive citation tracing, and included peer-reviewed English-language studies in K-12 or undergraduate settings that focused on teaching or promoting AI-related skills or awareness. From these studies, they derived a conceptual framework with three ways of understanding AI—technical details, tools, and sociocultural impact—and three ways of understanding literacy—functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial. They then organized the reviewed literature according to these combinations and compared pre-generative-AI and post-generative-AI trends.

The review covers studies conducted across K-12 and undergraduate education globally. In K-12, the literature prominently includes machine learning curricula, AI ethics instruction, and comprehensive curricula combining technical and sociocultural content. In higher education, pre-generative-AI work was relatively sparse, but post-2023 studies increasingly focused on teaching effective use of generative AI tools, especially prompt engineering and critical use of ChatGPT-like systems. The paper also notes age-related access restrictions for some generative AI tools that may constrain direct K-12 use.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy is best understood as an umbrella term spanning substantially different objectives and approaches, and that more precise terminology is needed. The authors find strong growth in studies treating AI as a tool, especially in postsecondary contexts after generative AI’s emergence, while K-12 work remains more centered on technical and sociocultural instruction. They conclude that the field now includes multiple distinct strands—such as machine learning education, AI ethics, and generative AI tool use—and that the proposed framework can help researchers and practitioners communicate more clearly about which form of AI literacy they are targeting and where important research gaps remain.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed integrative review that synthesizes 124 AI literacy studies, but it is not a meta-analysis of a specific intervention and does not provide causal estimates for K-12 generative AI literacy outcomes. For the requested K-12 generative-AI-and-literacy question, it offers only indirect, narrative evidence rather than direct outcome evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate a specific intervention effect on student literacy outcomes, so impact on K-12 literacy is unclear. Its contribution is conceptual and descriptive rather than demonstrating measurable academic impact.
